title: Latria and dulia: a school distinction both sides can tolerate
source_text: LIII. Illud quoque a nobis ostensum, Doctores Scholae Romanae fateri, distinctionem cultus Religiosi in Latriam & Duliam esse Scholae inventum; nec vocum istarum discrimen, prout in Schola Romana usurpantur, in Scriptura exacte servari: Duliam enim saepius ad cultum Deo proprium restringi, Latriam vero aliquando ad servitium humanum extendi. Vicissim autem Scholae Reformatae Doctores non multum repugnare, quin distinctionis causa, Latria divino cultui, Dulia vero observantiae illi, qua creaturae coli possunt & debent, accommodetur.
pass_a_gloss: This too has been shown by us, that the Doctors of the Roman School confess that the distinction of Religious worship into Latria and Dulia is an invention of the School; nor is the difference of those words, as they are used in the Roman School, exactly kept in Scripture: for Dulia is more often restricted to the worship proper to God, but Latria sometimes extended to human service. In turn, however, the Doctors of the Reformed School do not much resist that, for the sake of distinction, Latria be fitted to divine worship, but Dulia to that observance by which creatures can and ought to be honored.
pass_b_english: We have also shown that the teachers of the Roman school admit that the division of religious worship into latria and dulia is an invention of the schools, and that Scripture does not strictly keep the difference between these words as the Roman school uses them. Dulia is more often confined there to the worship proper to God, while latria is sometimes extended to service rendered to human beings.

The teachers of the Reformed school, for their part, do not much object if, for clarity's sake, latria is assigned to divine worship and dulia to the respect with which creatures may and should be honored.

choices.why: Technical terms kept as is; the thesis is about the words themselves.
